claims.claim: Origen of Alexandria was an early Christian theologian and biblical scholar, born c. 185 and died c. 253–254.
Origen was head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria and later founded the Christian School of Caesarea.
Only two of Origen's letters survive: one to Julius Africanus and one to Gregory Thaumaturgus.
The Letter to Africanus was written in response to Africanus's letter about the History of Susanna in the Book of Daniel, defending the authenticity of the Greek additions to Daniel.
Origen wrote the Letter to Africanus from Nicomedia, noting he had only a few days there to compose his reply.
The Letter to Gregory was written about 235 CE, after Origen had fled from persecution under Maximinus Thrax to Cappadocia, while Gregory had gone to Egypt.
The Letter to Gregory was addressed to Gregory Thaumaturgus, who later became bishop of Caesarea, and was preserved in the Philocalia compiled by Gregory of Nyssa and Basil of Caesarea.
In the Letter to Gregory, Origen urged his former pupil to apply Greek philosophy, geometry, and astronomy as preparatory studies for the interpretation of Holy Scripture.
Gregory Thaumaturgus had been Origen's pupil at Caesarea for several years before this letter was written.
The Panegyric on Origen, delivered by Gregory Thaumaturgus about 239 CE, shows that Origen's teaching had been successful.
The Letter to Africanus engages in early textual criticism, comparing Hebrew and Greek copies of the Book of Daniel.
